title: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis (2018)
summary: The Federal Arbitration Act requires courts to enforce employment arbitration agreements that call for one-on-one proceedings as written; the FAA's saving clause does not rescue a defense aimed at individualized arbitration, and NLRA section 7 does not clearly and manifestly displace the FAA.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 2018. Key line: "It is this Court's duty to interpret Congress's statutes as a harmonious whole rather than at war with one another." (Justice Gorsuch)

sections.Parties: Three consolidated cases pit employers against employees who signed arbitration agreements requiring individualized proceedings. Epic Systems Corporation, a Wisconsin software company, is petitioner against employee Jacob Lewis (No. 16-285). Ernst & Young LLP is petitioner against Stephen Morris, a former junior accountant who alleged the firm misclassified junior accountants and withheld overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act and California law (No. 16-300). In the third case the National Labor Relations Board is petitioner against Murphy Oil USA (No. 16-307). The employees, supported by the Board, argued that class and collective action waivers are illegal under the NLRA. The Solicitor General disavowed the Board's position and filed on the employers' side, so the government's own briefs were at odds.
sections.Material Facts: Ernst & Young and Morris agreed to arbitrate any disputes, with the employee choosing the provider and claims of different employees heard in separate proceedings. After his employment ended Morris sued in federal court, seeking a nationwide FLSA collective action under 29 U.S.C. section 216(b) and a Rule 23 class on the state claim. Epic emailed its employees an agreement stating that anyone who continued working at Epic would be deemed to have accepted individual arbitration of wage claims. The FAA dates from 1925 and the NLRA from 1935. In 2010 the Board's general counsel opined in Memorandum GC 10-06 that such agreements do not involve NLRA policies. In 2012, for the first time in 77 years, the Board held that the NLRA nullifies class waivers. Rule 23 did not create the modern class action until 1966. Mandatory arbitration covered 2.1 percent of nonunion employees in 1992 and 53.9 percent in 2017.
sections.Procedural History: In Ernst & Young, the district court granted the motion to compel arbitration, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the FAA's saving clause excuses enforcement when an agreement violates another federal law and that individualized arbitration bars the concerted activity protected by the NLRA; Judge Ikuta dissented. The Seventh Circuit, in an opinion by Judge Wood, reached the same result in Epic Systems. The Fifth Circuit disagreed in Murphy Oil and refused to enforce the Board's order. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in all three cases to resolve the split. It reversed the Seventh and Ninth Circuits in Nos. 16-285 and 16-300, affirmed the Fifth Circuit in No. 16-307, and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Issue: Whether an employer and employee may agree that disputes between them will be resolved through one-on-one arbitration, or whether employees must always be permitted to bring class or collective actions. Two statutory questions follow. First, whether the FAA's saving clause, which lets courts refuse enforcement on "such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract," covers a defense that class waivers are illegal under the NLRA. Second, whether section 7 of the NLRA, which protects "other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection," clearly and manifestly overrides the FAA's command to enforce arbitration agreements according to their terms.
sections.Holding: Courts must enforce the arbitration agreements as written, including their terms for individualized proceedings. The saving clause recognizes only defenses that apply to any contract, and under Concepcion a defense that targets the individualized nature of arbitration interferes with a fundamental attribute of arbitration whether it sounds in unconscionability or illegality. The NLRA does not supply a clear and manifest command to displace the FAA: section 7 speaks to organizing and collective bargaining, says nothing about class or collective procedures, and its catchall phrase is limited by the specific terms that precede it. The two statutes can be read in harmony, so that is where the Court's duty lies. Five Justices joined the opinion; four dissented.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Gorsuch combined text, precedent, and harmonizing canons. FAA sections 2, 3, and 4 direct courts to enforce arbitration agreements and their chosen procedures, and Concepcion held that the saving clause cannot save a defense that conditions enforcement on classwide procedures, whether the defense is called illegality or unconscionability. On the NLRA, Morton v. Mancari and Fausto require giving effect to both statutes, with a strong presumption against implied repeal absent clear and manifest intent. Section 7's catchall for "other concerted activities" follows a list about organizing, joining unions, and bargaining, so ejusdem generis confines it to things employees do for themselves at work, not courtroom procedure. The NLRA's structure regulates each listed activity in detail but is silent about class procedures; Congress overrides the FAA expressly in other statutes; and Whitman forbids hiding elephants in mouseholes. Gorsuch rejected legislative history outright, quoting Justice Jackson that "legislative history is not the law." Justice Ginsburg's dissent reasoned from purpose and history: the NLRA answered the bargaining imbalance workers face, and for over 75 years the Board treated joint suits as protected. She argued the FAA was written for merchants, that illegality is a generally applicable defense, that the later and more specific NLRA controls any conflict, and that the ruling will cause underenforcement of wage laws.

topics.lrs-k-implied-repeal: The Court requires a clear and manifest congressional intention before one statute displaces another and finds none in section 7, while the dissent argues the later and more specific NLRA should repeal the FAA to the extent of any conflict.
topics.lrs-k-ejusdem: The catchall "other concerted activities" is read in light of the specific terms about organizing and bargaining that precede it; the dissent objects that the canon should not narrow deliberately broad language.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The case stages competing canons: harmony and the presumption against implied repeal on one side, the later-in-time and specific-over-general rules on the other, with each side claiming its canon fits.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: Gorsuch refuses to consult legislative history, saying it is not the law, while Ginsburg builds her reading on the NLRA's history and the 1924 hearings on the FAA.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The majority infers from the NLRA's detailed regulation of every other section 7 activity that Congress did not silently protect class procedures, and treats express FAA overrides in other statutes as a benchmark.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Gorsuch wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, a 5 to 4 vote. Justice Thomas concurred, adding that the saving clause reaches only defenses concerning formation of the agreement and that illegality is a public-policy defense outside it. Justice Ginsburg dissented, joined by Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan, arguing that section 7 protects collective litigation, that employer-imposed waivers are unfair labor practices under section 8(a)(1), and that the Court's expansion of the FAA far beyond merchant contracts has revived the yellow-dog contract.
learning.why: Epic Systems is the modern textualist counterpoint to Train: the majority resolves a claimed conflict between two statutes with the presumption against implied repeal, ejusdem generis, structural inference, and the "Congress knows how to say so" canon, and it says outright that legislative history is not the law, while the dissent shows the purposive method those tools displace.
